notes: Part I insurance trial on uPVC pinking claims; coverage, LNO and knowledge issues all resolved against Tioxide.

enrichment.short_title: Tioxide v insurers: claims-made cover for titanium dioxide pinking liability
key_facts: Tioxide supplied R-TC30 and R-TC4 titanium dioxide pigments used in uPVC window products that pinked in certain outdoor conditions with all-lead stabilisers.
Multiple substantial pinking claims were settled confidentially; Tioxide sought indemnity under 1996/7 primary and excess claims-made liability policies.
Tioxide exercised the Loss Notification Option in the primary policy in July 1997 but excess insurers disputed valid LNO exercise and coverage.
Insurers argued the claims were not for Property Damage resulting from a single Loss and that Tioxide expected further pinking from March 1994.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Part I split trial of coverage, notification and knowledge issues under excess layer global liability policies before Morison J.
enrichment.outcome: Tioxide's indemnity claim wholly failed: no single Loss within the policy definition, excess LNO not validly exercised, and post-March 1994 supplies excluded as expected Property Damage.
enrichment.ratio: Claims-made product liability cover requires damages on account of Property Damage resulting from an identifiable accident or harmful condition; a manufacturer's continuing supply error is not a single aggregating Loss, and an LNO in excess policies must strictly comply with its terms including addressee and timing.
legal_issues: Whether pinking claims were damages on account of Property Damage
Whether all pinking claims arose from a single Loss or accident
Whether Tioxide validly exercised the Loss Notification Option in primary and excess policies
Whether Property Damage from continued pigment supplies was expected by Tioxide
linked_authorities: Fraser v B.N. Furman [1967] 2 Lloyd's Rep 1
Sofi v Prudential Assurance [1993] 2 Lloyd's Rep 559

notes: Second judicial review in McCann domestic violence tenancy saga; Court of Appeal ratio held binding.

enrichment.short_title: McCann v Birmingham: notice to quit after domestic violence re-housing
key_facts: Mr and Mrs McCann held a joint secure tenancy at 9 Anstey Grove; Mrs McCann left after domestic violence and was re-housed by Birmingham City Council.
Mrs McCann returned keys in August 2001; the Council later obtained a notice to quit from her in January 2002 without explaining its effect on Mr McCann.
Mr McCann returned to renovate the property and applied to exchange tenancies but the Council refused alternative accommodation and commenced possession.
The Court of Appeal had already held Article 8 could not defeat possession after a valid notice to quit terminated the joint tenancy.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of Council decisions to procure Mrs McCann's notice to quit and to refuse alternative accommodation before possession proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Application refused; the Council acted lawfully within its domestic violence policy and the Court of Appeal had already determined the public law challenges.
enrichment.ratio: Obtaining a notice to quit from a leaving joint tenant to end a secure tenancy after domestic violence re-housing is not an unlawful circumvention of Ground 2A possession proceedings; Article 8 does not defeat proprietary possession rights after valid termination.
legal_issues: Whether the Council unlawfully sidestepped Housing Act 1985 possession procedures
Whether the Council acted ultra vires its domestic violence and allocations policies
Whether procuring the notice to quit without advising Mrs McCann was procedurally improper
Whether refusing alternative accommodation breached Article 8
linked_authorities: Bradney v Birmingham City Council, Birmingham City Council v McCann [2003] EWCA Civ 1783
London Borough of Newham v Kibata [2003] EWCA Civ 1785
Harrow London Borough Council v Qazi [2003] UKHL 43

notes: Forum non conveniens stay of English declaratory proceedings; WTC business interruption insurance dispute.

enrichment.short_title: RSA v Retail Brand: stay of Master Policy proceedings in favour of New York
key_facts: Brooks Brothers' One Liberty Plaza store was damaged in the 11 September 2001 World Trade Centre attack.
Retail Brand claimed about $13.6m business interruption under a Delaware Local Policy and alternatively under an English-law Master Policy.
RSA and subsidiary RIC commenced parallel declaratory proceedings in England and New York on the same day in April 2004.
Retail Brand sought a stay of the English proceedings, arguing New York was the natural forum for both policies.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application to stay English proceedings for declaratory relief on the Master Policy after service out of the jurisdiction.
enrichment.outcome: Stay granted; New York was the natural forum despite the Master Policy's English governing law clause.
enrichment.ratio: Where Local and Master policy disputes overlap after a New York loss and insurers themselves chose New York for the Local Policy, the convenience of single case management at the loss location outweighs the limited significance of an English law clause absent an exclusive jurisdiction agreement.
legal_issues: Whether England or New York was the natural forum for Master Policy construction disputes
Weight to be given to an English law governing clause without a jurisdiction clause
Whether parallel English and New York proceedings should be consolidated in one forum
Whether RSA/RIC acted cynically by splitting proceedings between jurisdictions
linked_authorities: New Hampshire Ins Co v Philips Electronics (No 1) [1999] vol 1 58

confidence.notes: Stay decision and reasoning on forum factors are explicit though policy construction issues were not resolved.

notes: Unless order striking out appeal for maintenance pending suit default; Moses-Taiga jurisdiction litigation.

enrichment.short_title: Moses-Taiga v Oghenerume: strike-out for non-payment of interim maintenance
key_facts: The husband obtained conditional permission to appeal Singer J's maintenance pending suit orders but failed to pay about £150,000 within seven days as required.
He also ignored warnings and paid nothing of the £25,000 monthly maintenance, leaving the wife and solicitors in severe financial difficulty.
The wife applied under CPR 52.9 to strike out the appeal unless arrears and future maintenance were paid.
A major jurisdiction and forum non conveniens hearing was listed for November 2004 in the Family Division.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application to strike out an appeal notice for breach of conditions attached to permission and non-payment of maintenance pending suit.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal notice to be struck out unless specified arrears, costs and September and October 2004 maintenance instalments were paid; £90,000 in joint account released to the wife's solicitors.
enrichment.ratio: Persistent breach of maintenance pending suit and conditions on permission to appeal, which obstruct the other party's ability to litigate, is a compelling reason under CPR 52.9(2) to strike out the appeal notice.
legal_issues: Whether non-payment of maintenance pending suit is a compelling reason to strike out an appeal
Scope of CPR 52.9 powers where the appellant was present when permission was granted
Whether the court could vary the stay on maintenance pending suit
Relationship between interim maintenance and equality of arms in family litigation
linked_authorities: Hammond Suddard Solicitors v Agrichem International Holdings Ltd [2001] EWCA Civ 2065
Carr v Barr Cotton [2002] EWCA Civ 789
Bell Electric Ltd v Aweco Appliance Systems GmbH & Co KG [2002] EWCA Civ 1501

notes: Interlocutory D&O insurance dispute; Black parties permitted to intervene, no stay of Part 24 application.

enrichment.short_title: Chubb v Davies: intervention by fraud victims in D&O indemnity claim
key_facts: Mr Davies, CEO of Brandeis Brokers, was found liable in deceit for fraudulent representations causing US$18.7m losses to Herbert Black and associated companies.
Chubb sought a declaration that a French-law D&O policy did not indemnify Davies and commenced Part 24 summary judgment proceedings.
The Black parties, prospective judgment creditors, applied to intervene and stay the application pending Davies' appeal.
Chubb funded Davies' appeal costs while disputing indemnity under policy exclusions and public policy.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Applications by judgment creditors to intervene as defendants and to stay Chubb's Part 24 summary judgment application pending appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Black parties permitted to intervene on basis of accepting English jurisdiction; stay refused and merits hearing listed for December 2004.
enrichment.ratio: Prospective judgment creditors may be joined under CPR 19.2 where they have a real interest in whether D&O insurance responds, even before rights under the 1930 Act accrue, and need not await the insured's bankruptcy.
legal_issues: Whether third parties without accrued 1930 Act rights could intervene
Whether French jurisdiction clause excluded English proceedings against the director
Whether Part 24 summary judgment should be stayed pending Davies' appeal
Whether intervention required submission to English jurisdiction
linked_authorities: Normid Housing Association v Ralphs [1989] 1 Lloyd's Rep 265
Wood v Perfection Travel Ltd [1996] LRLR 233

notes: Divisional Court quashed Crown Court sentence increase for irrelevant magistrates' committal factor.

enrichment.short_title: Lees-Sandey: Crown Court unlawfully increased indecent assault sentence
key_facts: The claimant pleaded guilty to three indecent assaults on young women in Bognor Regis and Hayling Island in February and March 2004.
Magistrates sentenced him to eight months' imprisonment consecutive, reflecting a guilty plea discount.
On appeal the Crown Court increased the total to twelve months, criticising the magistrates for retaining jurisdiction instead of committing for sentence.
The Divisional Court reviewed whether the increase was wrong in law or exceeded jurisdiction.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of a Crown Court decision on appeal against sentence to increase an indecent assault term from eight to twelve months.
enrichment.outcome: Crown Court decision quashed; original eight-month magistrates' sentence restored.
enrichment.ratio: A Crown Court may not increase sentence on appeal because it considers the magistrates should have committed the case for sentence; such an irrelevant consideration constitutes an error of law warranting quashing.
legal_issues: Whether a twelve-month sentence for three indecent assaults was outside jurisdiction
Whether consecutive sentences for two same-day offences against different victims were wrong in principle
Whether reliance on the magistrates' failure to commit for sentence was an error of law
Standard for Divisional Court intervention in Crown Court sentencing appeals
linked_authorities: R v Truro Crown Court ex parte Adair [1997] Crown Office Digest 296
R v DPP ex parte McGeary [1999] Crim LR 430
Amin [1998] 1 Cr App R(S) 63

notes: Bankruptcy sale appeal; Re Citro exceptional circumstances test upheld despite HRA Article 8 argument.

enrichment.short_title: Barca v trustee: bankruptcy possession and sale of family home

statutes_considered.title: Trusts of Land and Appointment of Trustees Act 1996

key_facts: Mr Barca was made bankrupt in 1995; the trustee sought possession and sale of 10 Prioress Road with substantial equity for creditors.
Mr Barca's son Lorenzo, with special educational needs, stayed with him several nights a week and relied on his father's support for schooling.
Former partner Beatrice de Cock claimed a beneficial interest from mortgage contributions but later withdrew her claim for lack of legal aid.
The Deputy Registrar ordered vacant possession by July 2004 after finding no exceptional circumstances under section 335A.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against Chancery Registrar order for possession and sale of bankrupt's home pending determination of beneficial interests.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; creditors' interests prevailed and no exceptional circumstances justified postponing sale despite Article 8 considerations.
enrichment.ratio: Under section 335A(3) the court assumes creditors' interests outweigh others unless circumstances are exceptional; disruption to a child's education in the usual bankruptcy context does not qualify, though HRA section 3 may require a broader proportionality reading of 'exceptional'.
legal_issues: Whether hardship to a special-needs child constituted exceptional circumstances
Whether sale should await determination of Ms de Cock's beneficial interest
Compatibility of Re Citro with Article 8 and Protocol Article 1
Whether section 335A or section 337 applied to the property
linked_authorities: Re Citro [1991] Ch 142
Re Holliday [1981] Ch 405
Claughton v Charalambous [1998] BPIR 558

notes: Single LJ granted security and half judgment sum payment-in under CPR 52.9; asset-stripping suspicion.

enrichment.short_title: Vodafone v GNT Holdings: security and payment-in on guarantee appeal
key_facts: Vodafone obtained judgment for about £535,000 against GNT Holdings on a guarantee signed by director Nicholas Barter.
Holdings defended on lack of authority under a board resolution requiring two directors' signatures for contracts over £100,000.
The judge found Barter had actual authority from CEO Malkus despite the resolution; Holdings appealed on a narrow legal point.
Holdings transferred its main asset, an 83% shareholding in a German subsidiary, to Swiss company Chepha shortly before Vodafone's winding-up petition.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Single Lord Justice applications for security for costs and payment into court of half the judgment sum under CPR 52.9 pending appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Security ordered at £16,500 and payment-in of £250,000 required by 8 October 2004, failing which the appeal would be struck out.
enrichment.ratio: Where an appellant appears to have rendered itself judgment-proof by divesting assets yet continues to fund an appeal, exceptional circumstances provide a compelling reason under CPR 52.9 to require payment-in of part of the judgment sum as well as security for costs.
legal_issues: Whether Holdings would be unable to pay costs if the appeal failed
Whether there was compelling reason under CPR 52.9(2) to order payment-in of the judgment sum
Whether asset transfers to Chepha were designed to defeat enforcement
Whether such orders would stifle an arguable appeal

notes: Authoritative Richards J judgment on non-reviewability of section 51 dismissal decisions.

enrichment.short_title: Snelgrove: judicial review of section 51 dismissal refusal unavailable
key_facts: Lee Snelgrove was sent to the Crown Court for trial on a section 18 wounding charge based largely on complainant Darren Reynolds' identification evidence.
Unused material disclosed inconsistent statements, a dropped-charges note and indications Reynolds suffered mental illness.
Judge Norris refused dismissal, adjournment for psychiatric evidence and reliance on crime reports, finding a prima facie case remained.
Snelgrove sought judicial review of those refusals under the section 51 dismissal procedure.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of Crown Court decisions refusing to dismiss a sent charge under Schedule 3 paragraph 2 Crime and Disorder Act 1998.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed for want of jurisdiction under section 29(3) Supreme Court Act 1981; on the merits the judge's approach would also have been lawful.
enrichment.ratio: A Crown Court decision on an application to dismiss a charge sent under section 51 is a matter relating to trial on indictment and not amenable to judicial review; weaknesses in prosecution evidence are for the trial process including no-case submissions.
legal_issues: Whether section 29(3) excludes judicial review of section 51 dismissal decisions
Whether the Crown Court acts as examining justices in the sent procedure
Whether crime reports and psychiatric material could be considered on dismissal
Whether refusal of adjournment breached Article 6 equality of arms
linked_authorities: R (Salubi and others) v Bow Street Magistrates' Court [2002] 2 Cr.App.R. 40
R v Central Criminal Court ex parte Director of Serious Fraud Office [1993] 1 WLR 949
R v Galbraith (1981) 73 Cr App R 124

notes: Gypsy site planning appeal; Court restored Inspector's Article 8 proportionality balancing after Chapman.

enrichment.short_title: Chichester gypsy site: Article 8 and planning permission appeal
key_facts: Three gypsy families occupied land at Clearwater, West Ashling with mobile homes without planning permission from about 1999.
Chichester District Council refused permissions and took enforcement action; a Secretary of State Inspector granted permission finding Article 8 violations.
Blackburne J quashed the Inspector's decision on Structure Plan policy, material considerations and Article 8 approach.
The Secretary of State and occupiers appealed, arguing the Inspector correctly balanced planning harm against gypsy accommodation needs.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from section 288 High Court judgment quashing an Inspector's planning permission for an unauthorised private gypsy site.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; the Inspector's Article 8 proportionality assessment was lawful and enforcement would be disproportionate, restoring planning permission.
enrichment.ratio: Following Chapman v UK, shortage of authorised gypsy sites is a relevant Article 8 factor but does not create a duty to grant permission; an Inspector may find enforcement disproportionate where refusal would leave families without suitable alternative accommodation.
legal_issues: Whether the Inspector misapplied Article 8 after Chapman v UK
Whether development breached Structure Plan policy on gypsy sites
Whether the Inspector adequately identified material considerations for Mr Eames
Interaction of section 54A and human rights in planning decisions
linked_authorities: Chapman v United Kingdom (2001) 33 EHRR 399
First Secretary of State v Wiltshire County Council [2004] EWCA Civ 1062

confidence.notes: Central Article 8 issue clearly resolved on appeal though subsidiary policy points were largely academic.
